items.title: Atomic radius goes UP across the lanthanides (then drops)
items.claim: Atomic radius generally decreases across a period: protons increase but the outer shell is the same. The 4f electrons in the lanthanides screen the nucleus so poorly that radius decreases throughout the row — and then the 5d and 6s elements after them are SMALLER than expected.
items.prompt: What's the consequence of this 'lanthanide contraction'?

options.text: Elements just after the lanthanides (Hf, Ta, W and below) have surprisingly small radii, almost identical to those of the elements above them in the same group (Zr, Nb, Mo) — so zirconium and hafnium have nearly identical chemistry and are very hard to separate
Atomic radius goes UP, not down, across the lanthanides

items.reveal:
Across the 14 lanthanides, atomic number rises by 14 but the added electrons go into 4f orbitals, which are 'inside' the 6s shell and screen the outer electrons very poorly. So the effective nuclear charge felt by the 6s shell grows steadily — the outer shell shrinks.

By the time you reach hafnium (Z=72, just after the lanthanides), the atomic radius is approximately the same as zirconium (Z=40) above it. Atomic radius is 159 pm for Zr, 156 pm for Hf — virtually identical.

The practical consequence: Zr and Hf are chemically almost indistinguishable and have to be separated by very fine techniques (typically ion-exchange chromatography). They are sold side by side. Hafnium controls in nuclear reactors depend on this.
items.why: Down-group similarity is taught; lateral similarity caused by f-shell shielding is a hidden consequence of the periodic table's full structure.

items.title: Going down a group does NOT always mean smaller ionisation energy
items.claim: First ionisation energies generally decrease down a group as the outer electron sits in a larger, more shielded orbital. Yet gold's first IE (890 kJ/mol) is HIGHER than silver's (731), and silver is higher than copper's (745) is debatable.
items.prompt: Why do the textbook trends break down here?

options.text: Relativistic contraction of the 6s orbital in heavy elements (gold, mercury) lowers the outer electron's energy, making it more tightly bound than a non-relativistic shielding picture would predict
Gold is not really in Group 11
Outer electrons of gold are pulled by nuclear charge alone

items.reveal:
Simple shielding arguments predict each row's outer electron should be easier to remove than the row above. They work moderately well for s-block and p-block. They fail for heavy transition metals and post-transition metals where relativistic effects matter.

Gold's 6s orbital contracts and becomes more 'core-like'. Its first ionisation energy rises. Mercury is similar.

Another counter-trend: across a period, IE generally rises, but boron < beryllium (because B's outer electron is in a higher-energy 2p, while Be's is in the lower 2s); oxygen < nitrogen (pairing penalty in O's half-filled 2p4 vs N's stable 2p3 half-filled).
items.why: Periodic trends are taught as smooth ladders. Real data has dips and bumps that diagnose deeper physics.

items.title: Hafnium and zirconium are almost impossible to tell apart
items.claim: Zirconium and hafnium sit one above the other in Group 4 — separated by the entire lanthanide row. They have almost identical atomic radii (160 vs 159 pm), nearly identical ionic radii, and remarkably similar chemistry.
items.prompt: Why doesn't hafnium have a larger radius like the down-group trend predicts?

options.text: Hafnium has fewer electrons than expected

The 14 lanthanide elements between them add 14 protons but the 4f electrons screen the nucleus very poorly, so the effective nuclear charge experienced by the 5d and 6s shells in Hf is much higher than down-group trends suggest — the 'lanthanide contraction'
Hafnium atoms are crushed by gravity

items.reveal:
Across the 14 lanthanides, atomic number rises by 14 but the added electrons go into 4f orbitals 'inside' the 6s shell. Because 4f electrons screen poorly, the outer electrons see steadily more effective nuclear charge — and the atomic radius shrinks across the row.

By the time you reach hafnium (Z=72), the radius is essentially the same as zirconium (Z=40, four periods up the table). The two elements are chemically near-identical and have to be separated by very fine techniques — typically ion exchange chromatography.

Nuclear reactor design depends on the separation. Zirconium is used for fuel-rod cladding (very low neutron absorption); hafnium has a neutron cross-section about 600 times higher and is used for control rods. Mixing them up is catastrophic.
items.why: Down-group similarity is taught; lateral similarity caused by f-shell shielding is a hidden consequence of the full periodic table.
